title: SQL on SQLite — function-by-function reference
intro_md:
Everything here runs on **SQLite** (via sql.js in your browser) against the fictional Saint Louis University dataset. Open the **Schema** drawer for tables, columns, keys and previews. Every example has a *Try in sandbox* button that loads and runs it.

> SQLite is not MySQL or Postgres. Differences that bite: no `PIVOT`, no `MEDIAN()`, no `YEAR()`/`DATE_PART` (use `strftime`), `||` for string concatenation (not `+` or `CONCAT`), `LIMIT n OFFSET m` instead of `TOP`, integer division for `INTEGER / INTEGER`, booleans are `0`/`1`, and `TRUE`/`FALSE` are just aliases for 1/0. Window functions, CTEs and recursive CTEs *are* supported.
sandbox_md: Free play on the whole database. All statements are allowed here (CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE…). Press **Reset DB** to reload the original file. Ctrl/Cmd+Enter runs; the last statement's result is shown.
sandbox_starter:
-- Full dataset, nothing graded. Try:
SELECT d.name AS department, COUNT(*) AS employees, ROUND(AVG(e.salary)) AS avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.name
ORDER BY employees DESC;

sections.heading: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT
sections.body_md: `SELECT` picks columns, `WHERE` filters rows *before* grouping, `ORDER BY` sorts (`DESC` for descending, several keys allowed), `LIMIT` caps the row count. `DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows. Text patterns: `LIKE 'M%'` (`%` = anything, `_` = one char, case-insensitive for ASCII in SQLite), `IN (...)`, `BETWEEN a AND b`.

examples.label: Filter + sort + limit
examples.code:
SELECT first_name, last_name, gpa
FROM students
WHERE home_state = 'IL' AND gpa >= 3.5
ORDER BY gpa DESC, last_name
LIMIT 10;

examples.label: DISTINCT with LIKE and IN
examples.code:
SELECT DISTINCT home_state, home_city
FROM students
WHERE home_state IN ('MO', 'KS') AND home_city LIKE 'S%'
ORDER BY 1, 2;

sections.heading: Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
sections.body_md: `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(col)` (ignores NULL), `COUNT(DISTINCT col)`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `GROUP_CONCAT(col, ', ')`. `GROUP BY` folds rows into groups; `HAVING` filters *groups* after aggregation (`WHERE` cannot see aggregates). `ROUND(x, 2)` for presentation.

examples.label: One-row summary
GROUP BY + HAVING
examples.code:
SELECT home_state, COUNT(*) AS n_students, ROUND(AVG(gpa), 2) AS avg_gpa
FROM students
GROUP BY home_state
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10
ORDER BY n_students DESC;

examples.label: GROUP_CONCAT
examples.code:
SELECT d.name, GROUP_CONCAT(m.name, ', ') AS majors
FROM departments d
JOIN majors m ON m.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.name
ORDER BY d.name;

sections.heading: Joins: INNER, LEFT, self-join, anti-join
sections.body_md: `JOIN ... ON` keeps matching rows only. `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULL when nothing matches — the basis of the **anti-join** pattern (`WHERE right.id IS NULL`). A **self-join** joins a table to itself under two aliases (employee ↔ manager). `USING (col)` is shorthand when both sides share the column name. SQLite has no `RIGHT JOIN` before 3.39 and no `FULL JOIN` — swap the table order instead.

examples.label: Inner join across three tables
examples.code:
SELECT c.course_code, t.name AS term, s.section_number, s.capacity
FROM sections s
JOIN courses c ON c.course_id = s.course_id
JOIN terms t ON t.term_id = s.term_id
WHERE c.course_code LIKE 'CSCI%'
ORDER BY t.term_id, c.course_code
LIMIT 15;

examples.label: Anti-join: departments with no employees
examples.code:
SELECT d.name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id
WHERE e.employee_id IS NULL;

examples.label: Self-join: employee and manager
examples.code:
SELECT e.first_name || ' ' || e.last_name AS employee, e.title,
       m.first_name || ' ' || m.last_name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.title LIKE 'Dean%';

sections.heading: Subqueries and CTEs
sections.body_md: A subquery can appear in `FROM` (derived table), in `WHERE ... IN (...)` / `EXISTS (...)`, or as a scalar in `SELECT`. A **CTE** (`WITH name AS (...)`) is the same idea with a name — easier to read and reusable within the statement. A *correlated* subquery references the outer row; `LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` in one gives "the second value".

examples.label: Scalar subquery vs CTE
examples.code:
WITH dept_avg AS (
  SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT e.last_name, e.salary, ROUND(a.avg_salary) AS dept_avg
FROM employees e
JOIN dept_avg a ON a.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE e.salary > a.avg_salary
ORDER BY e.salary DESC
LIMIT 10;

examples.label: EXISTS
examples.code:
SELECT c.course_code, c.title
FROM courses c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sections s WHERE s.course_id = c.course_id)
ORDER BY c.course_code;

sections.heading: CASE and conditional aggregation
sections.body_md: `CASE WHEN cond THEN x WHEN cond2 THEN y ELSE z END` is SQL's if/else. Inside `SUM(...)` it counts rows that satisfy a condition — the standard way to build a pivot-like table in SQLite, which has no `PIVOT`/`FILTER`.

examples.label: Bucketing
examples.code:
SELECT CASE WHEN gpa >= 3.5 THEN 'honors' WHEN gpa >= 3.0 THEN 'good' WHEN gpa IS NULL THEN 'no gpa' ELSE 'below' END AS band,
       COUNT(*) AS n
FROM students
GROUP BY band
ORDER BY n DESC;

examples.label: Conditional aggregation (pivot by hand)
examples.code:
SELECT t.name AS term,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.status = 'dropped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS dropped,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.status = 'enrolled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS in_progress
FROM enrollments e
JOIN sections s ON s.section_id = e.section_id
JOIN terms t ON t.term_id = s.term_id
GROUP BY t.term_id
ORDER BY t.term_id;

sections.heading: Window functions
sections.body_md: `func() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame)` computes a value per row *without* collapsing rows. Ranking: `ROW_NUMBER()` (1,2,3,4), `RANK()` (1,1,3,4), `DENSE_RANK()` (1,1,2,3). Offsets: `LAG(col)`, `LEAD(col)`. Aggregates as windows: `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` is a running total; `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` is a 3-row moving window. Window functions are not allowed in `WHERE` — wrap them in a CTE and filter outside.

examples.label: RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER
examples.code:
SELECT last_name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_num,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 1
ORDER BY salary DESC;

examples.label: Top-N per group
Running total and LAG
examples.code:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', paid_on) AS month, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM tuition_payments WHERE status = 'posted' GROUP BY month
)
SELECT month, total,
       SUM(total) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running_total,
       total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change_vs_prev
FROM m ORDER BY month;

sections.heading: Recursive CTEs
sections.body_md: `WITH RECURSIVE name(cols) AS (base UNION ALL step)` walks hierarchies and graphs: org charts (`manager_id`), prerequisite chains, date series. The step selects from `name` itself; it stops when the step returns no rows. Always carry a `depth` column and guard against cycles (`WHERE depth < 20`) while experimenting — an unbounded recursion is killed after 15 s here.

examples.label: Org chart under the Provost
examples.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org(employee_id, name, depth) AS (
  SELECT employee_id, first_name || ' ' || last_name, 0
  FROM employees WHERE title = 'Provost'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name || ' ' || e.last_name, org.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN org ON e.manager_id = org.employee_id
)
SELECT depth, name FROM org ORDER BY depth, name LIMIT 30;

examples.label: Prerequisite chain
examples.code:
WITH RECURSIVE pre(course_id, depth) AS (
  SELECT p.prereq_course_id, 1 FROM course_prerequisites p
  JOIN courses c ON c.course_id = p.course_id WHERE c.title = 'Machine Learning'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.prereq_course_id, pre.depth + 1
  FROM course_prerequisites p JOIN pre ON pre.course_id = p.course_id
)
SELECT c.course_code, c.title, MIN(depth) AS depth
FROM pre JOIN courses c ON c.course_id = pre.course_id
GROUP BY c.course_id ORDER BY depth, course_code;

examples.label: Generate a series
examples.code:
WITH RECURSIVE n(x) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 10)
SELECT x, x * x AS square FROM n;

sections.heading: Strings, dates and NULL in SQLite
sections.body_md: Strings: `||` concatenates, `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `TRIM(x)` / `TRIM(x, chars)`, `SUBSTR(x, start, len)`, `LENGTH`, `REPLACE(x, from, to)`, `INSTR(x, needle)`, `GLOB` (case-sensitive wildcard with `*`, `?`, `[0-9]`). Dates are ISO text: `strftime('%Y', d)` year, `'%m'` month, `'%Y-%m'` month key, `date(d, '+30 days')`, `julianday(a) - julianday(b)` for day differences. NULL: `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` (never `= NULL`), `COALESCE(a, b, ...)` first non-null, `IFNULL(a, b)`, `NULLIF(a, b)` turns a placeholder into NULL. Aggregates skip NULL; `COUNT(*)` does not.

examples.label: Date parts and arithmetic
examples.code:
SELECT first_name, hire_date,
       strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS hire_year,
       CAST((julianday('2025-01-01') - julianday(hire_date)) / 365.25 AS INTEGER) AS years_of_service
FROM employees
ORDER BY hire_date LIMIT 10;

examples.label: COALESCE and NULLIF
examples.code:
SELECT s.student_id, COALESCE(e.last_name, '(no advisor)') AS advisor,
       NULLIF(s.gpa, 0) AS gpa
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = s.advisor_id
WHERE s.advisor_id IS NULL
LIMIT 10;

sections.heading: SQLite vs MySQL / PostgreSQL cheat-sheet
sections.body_md:
| Task | SQLite (here) | MySQL | PostgreSQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| concat | `a \|\| b` | `CONCAT(a, b)` | `a \|\| b` |
| year of date | `strftime('%Y', d)` | `YEAR(d)` | `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)` |
| median | window trick (see Hard 5) | none | `PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5)` |
| integer division | `7 / 2 = 3` | `7 / 2 = 3.5` | `7 / 2 = 3` |
| limit | `LIMIT n OFFSET m` | same | same |
| boolean | 0 / 1 | 0 / 1 | `true` / `false` |
| pivot | CASE + SUM | CASE + SUM | `FILTER (WHERE …)` or crosstab |
| string case in LIKE | case-insensitive (ASCII) | depends on collation | case-sensitive (`ILIKE`) |
| `RIGHT/FULL JOIN` | RIGHT since 3.39; no FULL | both | both |

Type affinity: SQLite stores whatever you insert; `CAST(x AS INTEGER)` / `CAST(x AS REAL)` convert explicitly.

examples.label: Integer division pitfall
examples.code: SELECT 7 / 2 AS integer_division, 7 / 2.0 AS real_division, CAST(7 AS REAL) / 2 AS cast_first;
